newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin silent on report Yeltsin to be discharged.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin silent on report Yeltsin to be discharged.

text.p: A Moscow radio station quoted a senior Kremlin source on Sunday as saying Boris Yeltsin would leave hospital on Tuesday but the Kremlin gave no news on the president's condition.

"President Boris Yeltsin's release from the Central Clinical Hospital has been set by the doctors' council for January 21," Ekho Moskvy radio said, adding that he would then go to one of his residences near Moscow to convalesce from double pneumonia.
At the Kremlin, which said on Friday Yeltsin would probably be discharged in the next few days, a spokesman told Reuters on Sunday: "I cannot comment. We have no information."
"There will be no information today," he added.

Ekho Moskvy said doctors were advising Yeltsin, who went into hospital on January 8, to cancel a visit to the Netherlands due on February 4. It would be his first foreign trip since he was re-elected last July.
The 65-year-old leader has not been seen in public since entering hospital. The last medical bulletin was on Friday.

"It (Yeltsin's discharge) will be in the next few days, but not at the weekend," press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said, adding that he assumed Yeltsin would attend a summit in Moscow of leaders of 12 former Soviet republics set for January 29.

The president has been reported to be working on documents and has had some official meetings and telephone conversations. Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin's improving health meant he would probably meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin this week.

A busy schedule, drawn up after Yeltsin's half-year absence preparing for and recovering from a heart bypass operation on November 5, includes receiving French President Jacques Chirac on February 2 and meeting Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, the European Union's current president, in the Hague on February 4.

Ekho Moskvy said Yeltsin wanted to go to the Netherlands, despite his doctors' advice. The chief Kremlin doctor has said publicly he has had to persuade Yeltsin to take things easy and has warned of a danger of complications from pneumonia.

Reports suggest Yeltsin is frustrated that he has not been able to return to work at full strength after his surgery, especially because Russia faces a host of problems, ranging from an epidemic of unpaid wages and pensions to rising tensions in Chechnya and responding to NATO's plans to expand eastwards.

Some analysts say the administrative machine is functioning smoothly in the president's absence. But Yeltisn's communist opponents in parliament and some would-be successors such as former security adviser Alexander Lebed say Russia is rudderless and have urged the president to step down.

In Chechnya, self-declared president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev accused the Kremlin of trying to sabotage the region's elections on January 27, previously agreed to by Moscow, which he hopes will give him a popular mandate to press for full independence.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana was due to arrive in Russia on Sunday with a package of measures aimed at softening the blow of NATO's planned expansion into eastern Europe, including a pledge of a permanent consultative forum between the two former foes.

Solana, asked by the Western alliance to negotiate a treaty or a charter with Moscow, will spend five hours with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Monday. But Russia seems set on wresting major concessions, so an early accord seems unlikely.
Hours before Solana flew in to Moscow, Itar-Tass news agency reported that the Russian air force was completing tests of a new frontline fighter, the Sukhoi Su-32.

Tass said it was "the weapon of the 21st century" and that it "outperforms the American F-15E". The Russian armed forces, starved of funds since the collapse of the Soviet Union, are keen to remind the West they are still a force to reckon with.
